idea: Anatomy-of plate of a double-storey lowercase 'g' in an old-style serif, each part labeled with a fine leader line (ear, upper bowl, link, lower loop, terminal), captioned 'Every letter has an ear.' It's a typographer's in-joke that also makes non-designers look twice at a letter they write every day.

A left-to-right lineage chart of the letter A: Egyptian ox-head hieroglyph, Proto-Sinaitic sign, Phoenician aleph, Greek alpha, Latin A, each rotated a little further, captioned 'Was once an ox.' Aleph really does mean ox, so it's a strange, true story told in five drawings.

Exploded engineering drawing of the type-caster's hand mould credited to Gutenberg: two interlocking halves, matrix, spring and a freshly cast sort, with part numbers and the caption 'The machine that made the machines.' It's for people who know that cheap, identical, reusable letters were the real invention.

The Indo-European language family as a botanical tree, with branches for Germanic, Italic, Celtic, Indo-Iranian, Slavic, Hellenic and others ending in living languages, captioned 'Your words are older than your country.' It gives English, Hindi, Persian and Welsh speakers a shared root, quietly.

Top-down plan of a printer's pair of type cases, capitals in the upper case and small letters in the lower case, every compartment labeled, titled 'Where lowercase comes from.' It's a real origin story hidden in a word everyone uses.

Cross-section of a hardcover book done like a medical cutaway (sewn signatures, spine, headband, joint, hinge, endpaper, board, fore-edge), with the caption 'Handle with care. Contains a person.' A bibliophile's anatomy plate that says why books are worth keeping.

Imposition diagram of one printed sheet showing where pages 1 to 16 land, half of them upside down, plus dotted fold lines turning it into an octavo signature, captioned 'One sheet. Sixteen pages. Fold in order.' It looks like an abstract puzzle and is actually how books were built.

Construction drawing of the interrobang, a question mark and an exclamation point overlaid on a grid with measurements, labeled 'Proposed by Martin Speckter, 1962. Still waiting.' It's for anyone who has typed '?!' and felt it deserved a better mark.

An evolution chart of the ampersand, from the Latin 'et' ligature in Roman cursive through medieval and italic forms to the modern '&', with a footnote saying the name comes from 'and per se and.' Eight drawings of one shape changing over two thousand years.

A clean Reed-Kellogg sentence diagram of Whitman's 'I am large, I contain multitudes.' with no other text. It quietly says the wearer contains multitudes, and grammar nerds will recognise the 1877 diagramming system right away.

A log-log chart of English word frequency following Zipf's law, with 'the', 'of', 'and', 'to' labeled at the top-left and the long tail running off to 'defenestrate', captioned 'Most words are rare. That's the point.' It's a quietly beautiful curve that sticks up for the unusual word.

Technical drawing of a Linotype keyboard with its first two columns picked out to read 'etaoin shrdlu', the letters arranged roughly by how often English uses them. The phrase was a real typesetter's mistake that sometimes slipped into newspapers, which makes it a deep-cut shirt for print people.

Schematic of the Rosetta Stone split into its three registers (hieroglyphic, Demotic, Greek), each bracketed and labeled, captioned 'Same decree, three scripts. Found 1799. Read 1822.' It's about how patient decipherment can be, told through a museum object everyone knows.

A sagittal cutaway of the human vocal tract, labeled like an instrument diagram (lips, teeth, alveolar ridge, hard palate, velum, uvula, tongue, glottis), titled 'Instrument for making meaning.' Anatomy and linguistics in one elegant plate.

A timeline schematic of movable type: Bi Sheng's clay type (1040s, China), the Jikji printed with metal type (1377, Korea), and Gutenberg's press (c. 1450s, Mainz), each with a small drawing, captioned 'Gutenberg was not first.' It corrects the usual story with true dates.

The Van de Graaf canon drawn as a construction diagram on an open two-page spread, diagonals crossing to place the text block in classic 2:3 page proportions, captioned 'The page was designed before the words.' It shows the hidden geometry behind beautiful books.

Plate showing how the basic Hangul consonants copy the speaking mouth: ㄱ as the tongue root against the throat, ㄴ as the tongue touching the gum ridge, ㅁ as the mouth, ㅅ as a tooth, ㅇ as the throat, each beside a small profile of a head. Captioned 'An alphabet that draws the mouth. King Sejong, 1446.' It's possibly the most rational writing system ever designed, explained in one picture.

A semantic-drift flowchart for the word 'nice': Latin nescius 'ignorant' to 'foolish' to 'shy' to 'fussy, precise' to 'pleasant', with arrows and approximate centuries, captioned 'Nice used to be an insult.' It's a smart, slightly sly shirt about how meanings change.

The ISO 216 paper-size diagram: an A0 sheet split recursively into A1, A2 and so on down to A8, with the √2 ratio and '1 m²' noted, captioned 'Cut it in half forever. It keeps its shape.' A spiral-like composition that sits well beside the golden-angle seed head and is true math on every office sheet.

A specimen paragraph thick with real proofreader's marks (deletes, carets, transpose loops, a struck-through word restored with dotted underlining and 'stet' in the margin), with a key below: 'stet: let it stand.' It's for writers and editors, and its point is that sometimes the first draft was right.
